courses.name: Economic Development
courses.format: In-class midterm. Bring your one-page, double-sided cheat sheet.
covers: Lecture 3: Hunger & nutrition traps (Poor Economics Ch 2)
Oct 14 lecture (check it’s not reading week)
cheat: North: institutions = 'the rules of the game', the humanly devised constraints that shape interaction. Formal (laws) vs informal (norms).
Inclusive = secure property rights, rule of law, open entry. Extractive = take from many to benefit a narrow elite.
AJR IV chain: settler mortality -> settlements -> early institutions -> current institutions -> GDP today. Exclusion restriction: mortality affects income ONLY through institutions.
Reversal of fortune: rich, dense colonies in 1500 got extractive institutions, so they're relatively poor today.
Poverty trap graph: income today (x) vs tomorrow (y) with a 45° line. S-curve below the line at low income = trap. Inverted L above the line = no trap.
Nutrition trap evidence: the poor buy tastier calories, not more calories. Jensen & Miller rice subsidy = Giffen behaviour.
Health: underinvestment in cheap prevention; small prices kill take-up of bed nets (Cohen & Dupas).
De-worming (Miguel & Kremer): spillovers, so randomize by school.
ATE = mean(treatment) - mean(control). Randomization removes selection bias.
traps: Drawing the S-curve and L-shape the wrong way round. Practise drawing both with the 45° line.
Saying settler mortality affects income directly. It's only through institutions.
Mixing up 'percent' and 'percentage points' in the ATE.
Forgetting the readings. Bolded readings are fair game.

links.t: MIT 14.73 (Banerjee & Duflo’s own course): quizzes with solutions
MIT 14.73 quiz 1 solutions (Giffen goods, Jensen & Miller)
MIT 14.73 lecture slides (nutrition, health, poverty traps)

q.q: Douglass North defines institutions as:
o: The rules of the game in a society: the humanly devised constraints that shape interaction
q.e: North: institutions are 'the rules of the game'. They can be formal (laws, constitutions) or informal (norms, customs).

q.q: Which is an INFORMAL institution?
o: A social norm about repaying debts within a village
q.e: Informal = unwritten norms, customs, codes of conduct. Formal = written rules backed by the state.

q.q: Extractive economic institutions are designed to:
o: Take income and wealth from many people to benefit a narrow elite
q.e: Extractive = concentrate power and wealth in a small group. Inclusive = secure property rights, rule of law, open entry, broad participation.

q.q: Which feature belongs to INCLUSIVE institutions?
o: Secure property rights and contracts for most people
Monopolies granted to the ruler's friends
q.e: Inclusive institutions give people incentives to invest and innovate because they keep what they earn.

q.q: In Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001), the instrument for institutions is:
q.e: Where early European settlers died a lot, they didn't settle. They set up extractive institutions instead.

q.q: Which chain is the AJR argument?
o: Settler mortality -> settlements -> early institutions -> current institutions -> income today
q.e: High mortality -> few settlers -> extractive early institutions -> they persist -> lower income today.

q.q: Why can't you just regress GDP on institutions to find the effect of institutions?
o: Reverse causality and omitted variables: richer countries may afford better institutions
q.e: That's the endogeneity problem. The instrument (settler mortality) shifts institutions for reasons unrelated to today's income.

q.q: The exclusion restriction in AJR says settler mortality affects income today:
o: Only through its effect on institutions
q.e: If old settler mortality affected income through some other channel (like today's disease burden), the IV estimate would be biased.

q.q: 'Reversal of fortune' means:
o: Colonies that were relatively rich in 1500 are relatively poor today
q.e: Rich, dense places got extractive institutions (easier to exploit). Sparse places got settlers and inclusive institutions, so the ranking flipped.

q.q: A poverty trap exists when the curve of income today vs income tomorrow is:
o: An inverted L shape that stays above the 45° line at low incomes
An S shape that is BELOW the 45° line at low incomes
q.e: S-curve: below the threshold, tomorrow's income < today's, so the poor get poorer and get stuck. Above it, people climb.

q.q: With an inverted-L (no trap) curve, a very poor person:
o: Still grows richer over time, because tomorrow's income is above today's at low levels
Needs a big push to escape
q.e: If the curve starts above the 45° line, everyone moves up toward the same steady state. No threshold, so no trap.

q.q: The nutrition-based poverty trap says:
o: People are too poor to eat enough to be productive, so they stay too poor to eat enough
q.e: Low income -> low calories -> low productivity -> low income. That's the S-curve logic applied to food.

q.q: Banerjee and Duflo find that when the very poor get a bit more money, they often:
o: Buy tastier, more expensive food (or TVs and festivals) instead of more calories
q.e: This is their main evidence that most people aren't stuck in a calorie-based trap.

q.q: Jensen and Miller subsidized rice in Hunan, China. Some very poor households:
o: Bought LESS rice and more meat/shrimp: Giffen behaviour
q.e: Cheaper rice freed up money, so people switched to tastier foods. Calories didn't go up.

q.q: Charging even a small price for bed nets (Cohen and Dupas) tends to:
o: Sharply cut take-up without getting nets to the people who need them most
q.e: Small fees -> big drop in demand, and paying didn't screen for the neediest. A key 'free vs cost-sharing' finding.

q.q: In the Kenya de-worming study (Miguel and Kremer), untreated kids in treatment schools also got healthier. That shows:
o: Externalities (spillovers): fewer worms around means less reinfection for everyone
q.e: That's why they randomized whole SCHOOLS, not individual kids. Individual randomization would underestimate the true effect.

q.q: In an RCT, average attendance is 82% in the treatment group and 75% in the control group. The ATE is:
q.e: ATE = mean(treatment) - mean(control) = 82 - 75 = 7 percentage points.

q.q: Why does random assignment give an unbiased estimate of the effect?
o: Treatment and control groups are the same on average before treatment, so there's no selection bias
q.e: Random assignment = no one chooses their group, so any later difference comes from the treatment.

q.q: Comparing kids whose parents CHOSE to buy deworming pills vs kids whose parents didn't would suffer from:
q.e: Parents who buy pills are probably different (richer, more informed), so the groups weren't comparable to begin with.

q.q: Banerjee and Duflo argue the poor underinvest in cheap prevention (chlorine, nets) partly because:
o: Benefits are in the future and invisible, while costs are now (plus beliefs and present bias)
They have no information at all
q.e: Cheap prevention has high returns but delayed, invisible payoffs. Curative care feels more valuable even when it isn't.

courses.name: Introduction to Astronomy
courses.format: 90 minutes. Multiple choice + short answer. No calculations.
covers: Intro: how science works, criteria for a theory
Light & telescopes (Ch 5 & 6): spectrum, spectra, Doppler, telescopes
The Solar System (Ch 16 & 17), the Oct 9 lecture
cheat: Theory checklist: explains observations, physically motivated and consistent, makes falsifiable predictions.
Light-year = distance. Looking far = looking back in time.
Kepler: 1) ellipses, Sun at one focus. 2) equal areas, fastest at perihelion. 3) farther = longer period.
Newton: inverse-square gravity. 2x distance = 1/4 force. Orbiting = free fall.
EM spectrum, low to high energy: radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma.
Hotter = bluer (Wien). Kirchhoff: continuous / emission / absorption.
Redshift = moving away. Aperture (area) matters most. Space telescopes beat the atmosphere.
Sun: H -> He fusion in the core. Layers: core, radiative, convective, photosphere, chromosphere, corona. Sunspots = cooler, magnetic, 11-year cycle.
Solar system: nebular theory (flat spinning disk), frost line -> rocky inside, giants outside.
traps: Magnification is not the most important telescope feature.

links.t: OpenStax Astronomy 2e: Ch 3 review questions (orbits & gravity)
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: Ch 5 review questions (light & spectra)
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: Ch 6 review questions (telescopes)
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: Ch 15 review questions (the Sun)
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: Ch 7 review questions (solar system)

q.q: A new astronomical theory should make novel predictions that are:
q.e: Falsifiable = there's an observation that could prove it wrong. That's criterion (c) from your intro lecture.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the three criteria a good theory should meet?
o: Be physically motivated and internally consistent
q.e: Popularity isn't a criterion. The three: explain observations, be physically motivated and consistent, make falsifiable predictions.

q.q: A light-year is a unit of:
q.e: A light-year is the DISTANCE light travels in one year (about 9.5 trillion km). Classic trick question.

q.q: Smallest to largest:
o: Solar System, Earth, Milky Way, Local Group
Earth, Solar System, Milky Way, Local Group
Earth, Milky Way, Solar System, Local Group
Earth, Solar System, Local Group, Milky Way
q.e: Planet -> planetary system -> galaxy -> group of galaxies -> cluster -> universe.

q.q: When you look at a galaxy 2 million light-years away, you see it:
o: As it was 2 million years ago
As it will be in 2 million years
As it was 2 million light-years ago, which is the same as now
q.e: Light takes time to travel. Looking far away = looking back in time.

q.q: Kepler's first law says planets orbit the Sun in:
o: Perfect circles centred on the Sun
Ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Ellipses with the Sun at the centre
q.e: Ellipse, Sun at ONE focus (not the centre). The other focus is empty.

q.q: By Kepler's second law, a planet moves fastest when it is:
o: At the same speed the whole time
q.e: Equal areas in equal times means it has to speed up when it's close to the Sun.

q.q: Kepler's third law tells us that planets farther from the Sun:
q.e: The bigger the orbit, the longer the period, and the period grows faster than the distance.

q.q: If the distance between two objects doubles, the gravity between them becomes:
q.e: Newton's law is an inverse SQUARE: 2x the distance -> 1/2² = 1/4 the force.

q.q: Astronauts on the ISS float because:
o: They're in constant free fall around Earth
q.e: Gravity at ISS height is still about 90% of surface gravity. They float because they and the station fall together around Earth.

q.q: Which list goes from LOWEST to HIGHEST energy?
o: Gamma, X-ray, UV, visible, infrared, radio
Radio, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma
Visible, radio, UV, infrared, gamma, X-ray
Radio, visible, infrared, UV, gamma, X-ray
q.e: Longer wavelength = lower frequency = lower energy. Radio is longest, gamma is shortest.

q.q: A star that looks blue compared to a red star is:
q.e: Wien's law: hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths, so they look bluer.

q.q: Cool, thin gas in front of a hot, dense light source produces:
q.e: Kirchhoff's laws: hot dense = continuous, hot thin gas = emission lines, cool gas in front of a hot source = absorption (dark) lines.

q.q: A galaxy's spectral lines are shifted toward longer wavelengths. It is:
q.e: Redshift = longer wavelength = moving away (Doppler effect). Blueshift = approaching.

q.q: The MOST important feature of a telescope for seeing faint objects is:
q.e: Light gathering grows with the area of the mirror. Double the diameter -> 4x the light.

q.q: The main reason to put telescopes in space is:
o: To get closer to the stars
Earth's atmosphere blurs images and blocks X-ray, UV and much infrared
Space is darker during the day only
q.e: Distance to the stars barely changes. The atmosphere is the problem: twinkling (blur) and absorption.

q.q: The Sun makes its energy by:
o: Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core
q.e: Nuclear fusion in the core: 4 hydrogen -> 1 helium, and the lost mass becomes energy (E = mc²).

q.q: Sunspots look dark because they are:
o: Hotter than the rest of the surface
q.e: They're still very hot, just cooler than their surroundings, caused by strong magnetic fields. The cycle is about 11 years.

q.q: The Sun doesn't collapse or explode because:
o: Its magnetic field holds it together
Gravity pulling in is balanced by gas pressure pushing out
q.e: Hydrostatic equilibrium: inward gravity = outward pressure, layer by layer.

q.q: Why are the giant planets far from the Sun?
o: They formed there because beyond the frost line ices could condense, giving them more solid material
They were pushed out by the solar wind
They're younger than the rocky planets
Gravity is stronger far from the Sun
q.e: Beyond the frost line, ices could freeze, so cores grew big enough to grab hydrogen and helium gas.

q.q: The nebular theory explains why planets:
o: Orbit in the same direction and in nearly the same plane
q.e: A spinning cloud flattened into a disk, so everything formed going the same way in roughly one plane.

courses.name: IT Infrastructure
courses.format: No devices at all, including calculators. Subnetting by hand.
covers: Ch 1: networking basics, OSI model, topologies, P2P vs client-server
Ch 3–4: addressing (MAC, IPv4, IPv6, ports, DHCP, DNS) and protocols (TCP/UDP)
Ch 7 (Oct 20 lecture) only if your prof says so
cheat: OSI top down: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. PDUs: data, segment, packet, frame, bits.
Switch = inside a network (MAC, L2). Router = between networks (IP, L3).
Ports: 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP.
DHCP = DORA. TCP = SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. UDP = no handshake.
Subnetting: block size = 256 − mask octet. Hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2. /25=128, /26=64, /27=32, /28=16, /29=8, /30=4.
Cat5e 1G/100m, Cat6 10G/~55m, Cat6a 10G/100m. SMF = laser, long. MMF = shorter.
2.4 GHz non-overlapping: 1, 6, 11. Wi-Fi = CSMA/CA. WPA3 (SAE) > WPA2 (AES).
traps: Subtracting 2 for hosts (network + broadcast) and forgetting it.

Professor Messer: free Network+ N10-009 course + pop quizzes
Professor Messer: Network+ pop quiz archive

q.q: Which device connects DIFFERENT networks and forwards traffic between them?
q.e: Rule of thumb from the slides: inside one network = switch, between networks = router.

q.q: IP addresses and routing happen at which OSI layer?
q.e: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing (IP) and routing. Layer 2 uses MAC addresses.

q.q: What is the PDU called at Layer 2?
q.e: Data (L5-7) -> Segment (L4) -> Packet (L3) -> Frame (L2) -> Bits (L1).

q.q: Every node connects directly to every other node. Which topology?
q.e: Full mesh = every node linked to every other. Most redundant, most expensive.

q.q: In a peer-to-peer network:
o: A central server controls all logins
Each computer manages its own resources and security
Only Windows Server can be used
Resources are shared through a domain controller
q.e: P2P has no central server. Each machine controls its own files and accounts. Cheap and simple, but doesn't scale and is hard to secure.

q.q: The MDF is:
o: A small closet on each floor
The main hub for the whole building's cabling, often near the entrance facility
q.e: MDF = main distribution frame (the central hub). IDFs are the smaller rooms on each floor that connect back to it.

q.q: What is the main point of change management?
o: To stop any change to the network
To make sure changes are approved, documented and can be rolled back
q.e: Change management controls risk: request, approve, schedule, document, and plan a rollback.

q.q: How long is a MAC address, and what are its first 24 bits?
q.e: MAC = 48 bits, written in hex. First 24 bits = OUI, which identifies the manufacturer.

q.q: Which address is PRIVATE?
A PC shows the address 169.254.33.7. What most likely happened?
o: It couldn't reach a DHCP server, so it assigned itself an APIPA address
q.e: 169.254.x.x = APIPA. Windows assigns it when DHCP fails. Usual fix: check the cable or DHCP server.

q.q: Which pair is correct?
q.e: Memorize: 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP.

q.q: What's the correct order of the DHCP process?
q.e: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

q.q: Which DNS record points a domain to its mail server?
q.e: A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias, MX = mail exchanger, PTR = reverse lookup.

q.q: The TCP three-way handshake is:
q.e: Client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client confirms with ACK.

q.q: Which statement about UDP is true?
o: It's connectionless and has no handshake, so it's faster
It's used for every web page
q.e: UDP = connectionless, no acknowledgments. Used for streaming, VoIP, DNS queries. TCP = reliable, connection-oriented.

q.q: What is the NETWORK address of 192.168.10.77/26?
What is the BROADCAST address of 192.168.10.77/26?
q.e: The block is 64-127. Broadcast = last address in the block = .127. Usable hosts are .65 to .126.

q.q: How many USABLE hosts does a /27 give you?
q.e: 32 - 27 = 5 host bits. 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 30.

q.q: What is the subnet mask for /28?
q.e: /28 = 24 + 4 bits in the last octet: 128+64+32+16 = 240.

q.q: Which cable supports 10 Gbps over the full 100 m?
o: Cat 6 (only up to about 55 m at 10G)
q.e: Cat 5e = 1 Gbps at 100 m. Cat 6 = 10 Gbps but only ~55 m. Cat 6a = 10 Gbps at 100 m.

q.q: Compared to multimode fiber, single-mode fiber:
o: Has a bigger core and is used for short runs
Uses a laser, has a tiny core and goes much longer distances
q.e: SMF: narrow core, laser light, long distance (km). MMF: wider core, LED/VCSEL, shorter runs inside buildings.

q.q: Which 2.4 GHz channels don't overlap?
q.e: In North America the only non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels are 1, 6 and 11.

q.q: Wi-Fi avoids collisions using:
q.e: Wireless = CSMA/CA (collision Avoidance). Old wired Ethernet = CSMA/CD (collision Detection).

q.q: Which is the strongest wireless security option?
q.e: WPA3 uses SAE, which protects against offline password guessing. WEP and TKIP are broken.

q.q: How long is an IPv6 address?
q.e: IPv6 = 128 bits in hex. :: can replace one run of zero groups, only once per address.

courses.name: Fundamentals of Programming
courses.format: 90 minutes, 40 multiple-choice questions, on paper. That's about 2 minutes per question. Expect 'what does this code print?', fill-in-the-blank code and data types.
covers: Class 4: repetition: while, for, range(), break/continue (Ch 5)
cheat: range(start, stop, step) stops BEFORE stop. range(5, 1, -1) = 5 4 3 2.
/ always gives a float. // = floor division. % = remainder. ** before * before +.
input() always returns a string. Convert with int() / float().
if/elif/else: only the FIRST true branch runs.
continue = skip to the next loop item. break = exit the loop now.
Slices include the start, exclude the stop. s[-1] = last char. s[::-1] = reversed.
Strings are immutable: s.upper() returns a new string.
b = a on a list makes an alias, not a copy.
No return statement = function returns None.
traps: Thinking print and return are the same.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: range(start, stop, step) stops BEFORE stop. Counting down from 5 with step -1, it stops before 1. Your prof flagged this exact pattern.
q.code:
for i in range(5, 1, -1):
    print(i, end=' ')

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Start at 2, add 3 each time: 2, 5, 8. The next one would be 11, but 11 is the stop value, so it's excluded.
q.code:
for i in range(2, 11, 3):
    print(i, end=' ')

q.q: What prints?
q.e: // is floor division (3), % is the remainder (1), / always gives a float (3.5).

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Exponent first: 4**2 = 16. Then 3*16 = 48. Then 2 + 48 = 50.

q.q:
The user types 5 at this prompt. What happens?

x = input('Number: ')
print(x + 1)
o: TypeError: can't add str and int
q.e: input() ALWAYS returns a string. '5' + 1 mixes str and int, so Python raises a TypeError. Fix: int(input(...)).

q.q: What prints? (This is the wordcount pattern your prof flagged.)
q.e: 'hi' counts (1). '#skip' hits continue, so it jumps to the next item without counting. 'done' hits break, so the loop ends. 'later' never runs. Final: 1.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: / always returns a float in Python 3, even when it divides evenly (6/2 = 3.0).

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Slices include the start index and exclude the stop. Index 1 = 'o', 2 = 'r', 3 = 'o'. Stop at 4.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: s[-1] is the last character ('o'), s[0] is the first ('T'). Joined: 'oT'.

Last valid index is len(s)-1. To include index 0, the stop has to be -1 (one past 0 going down). range(len(s), 0, -1) starts out of range, range(len(s)-1, 0, -1) misses index 0, and range(0, len(s), -1) prints nothing.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: b = a doesn't copy the list. Both names point to the SAME list, so appending through b changes a too.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: The function calculates x*2 but never returns it. A function with no return gives back None.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Only the FIRST true branch of an if/elif/else chain runs. x > 10 is true, so it prints A and skips the rest.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: This is the 'find the largest' loop pattern from the slides. None means 'nothing seen yet', then it keeps the bigger number each time.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Multiplying a string by an int repeats it.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: The inner list [2, 3] counts as ONE element. Three elements total.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: int() can't convert the string '3.5' (it has a decimal point), so it raises ValueError and jumps straight to except. 'ok' never prints.

q.q: How many stars print?
q.e: Nested loops multiply: 3 outer x 2 inner = 6 stars.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: find() returns the index where the match starts. P=0, y=1, t=2.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: split() with no argument splits on any run of spaces, so the double space doesn't create an empty item. 3 words, last is 'blue'.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: 1 -> 3 -> 9 -> 27. At 27 the condition n < 20 is false, so the loop stops and prints 27.
q.code:
n = 1
while n < 20:
    n = n * 3
print(n)

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Empty string and 0 are 'falsy'. Any non-empty string is True, even the text 'False'.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Strings are immutable. upper() RETURNS a new string, but nothing saved it, so s is still 'hello'.

q.q: What prints?
q.e: Slice 1:4 gives indexes 1, 2, 3. -2: means 'from the second-last to the end'.
